Internet Shutdowns in the Era of Digital India

By Ava Gough
On July 1, 2015, Prime Minister Narendra Modi launched Digital India, an initiative meant to foster a more digitally empowered society and knowledge-based economy, with broadband internet connectivity as one of its key pillars.
Earlier this month, Modi celebrated the movement’s progress on its 11th anniversary via X, claiming that more than a billion Indians have embraced technology and that the country boasts nearly 103 crore (about 1.03 billion) internet connections.
Photos: The images display Prime Minister Modi’s posts to X celebrating 11 years of Digital India.
In the years following the implementation of Digital India, the number of internet users in the country have grown significantly, reflecting the importance connectivity plays in India’s society today.
Despite these digital strides, India has one of the world’s highest rates of internet shutdowns, which are the intentional disruptions to internet access and digital communications.
At the time of this report, over 900 partial or full internet shutdowns have occurred in the country since 2016, a trend that stands in stark contrast to Digital India’s emphasis on nationwide connectivity.
These numbers come from Access Now’s Shutdown Tracker Optimization Project (STOP), which documents internet shutdowns across 100 countries. Their data also shows that India has undergone more shutdowns than any country it has tracked, and that nearly 70% of them have occurred in just 3 regions over the last decade.
The Concentration of India’s Shutdowns
How do internet shutdowns work in India?
According to Access Now, internet shutdowns are often implemented by governments to restrict the flow of information and to silence, punish or stoke fear in certain communities.
In India, the two main causes for these shutdowns, protests and political instability, account for about 47% of the country’s 920 shutdowns recorded in the STOP dataset.
The government justifications used for implementing these shutdowns tend to differ in language from the true causes behind them, framing their decisions in a more forward-looking and preventative way.
The authorities who order these shutdowns and provide these justifications are most often the state and local governments of the affected regions, with state authorities responsible for an estimated 512 shutdown operations and local governments accounting for 276 of them. Together, they make up about 86% of shutdown initiators recorded in the dataset, while the executive government has only been responsible for 24 shutdowns.
These national patterns do not look the same for every state or union territory, though, with the three internet shutdown hotspots experiencing these events under very different circumstances.
Jammu and Kashmir Shutdowns: Prolonged and Persistent
Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) is a union territory located in the Himalayas and is home to a projected population of just under 14 million residents. Since 2016, Access Now has recorded an estimated 468 internet shutdowns in the region, which has been the source of a decades long territory dispute between India and Pakistan.
Until 2019, J&K was long considered a semi-autonomous state due to these territorial disagreements. That year, on August 5, India's government announced its decision to strip its portion of the region’s special status to integrate it more into the country, which Modi and the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) claimed would improve J&K’s development.
As this decision was being passed, J&K entered into what would become one of the longest internet shutdown periods ever recorded in a democracy, with the entire region being placed in a total blackout for 6 months. In January 2020, the region received 2G data, putting it in a partial shutdown until February 2021 when 4G was reinstalled, making the entire event 18 months long.
Information received by the United Nations during the start of the shutdown suggested that journalists, human rights defenders, protesters and other residents were arrested, with its experts calling the shutdown a form of collective punishment and these detentions human rights violations.
As the shutdown persisted, journalists continued to struggle to get information out about the state of the union territory. Reuters said that some local newsrooms would have to send a team member to Delhi to fill in blanks where they couldn’t verify information for stories, and that one journalist they spoke to would drive to the airport in J&K’s capital to call friends in Delhi in order to deliver his reports and have his emails read to him. Others had their businesses shut down, were forced to move to access education and struggled to receive necessary healthcare.
Today, the region’s overall development continues to be hindered as shutdowns and communication restrictions persist.
Currently, J&K remains in another record long shutdown, this time, in the form of a communications blockade. The region lost 14 messaging apps in May 2023, and, according to the STOP dataset, this was to control information in the area, although the government claim it is for national security and counter-terrorism efforts.
Rajasthan Shutdowns: Short and Sporadic
Rajasthan is located in the northwest part of India and has a projected population just shy of 84 million people. It has experienced an estimated 77 shutdowns to date, making it the region with the second highest frequency. Unlike J&K, Rajasthan’s shutdowns are much shorter and not as frequent, lasting an average of less than 3 days.
Its longest shutdown event recorded by Access Now began on October 30, 2020 and ended on November 12, lasting a total of 14 days across four districts: Bharatpur, Karauli, Jaipur and Sawai Madhopur.
The shutdown included the suspension of mobile internet services and was said to be in reaction to reservation protests by the Gujjar community, an ethnic group located across northern and western India.
While protests like these and communal violence top the actual causes behind shutdowns in the region, Rajasthan is also known to switch off internet during exams, and is the only region of the top three to do so.
In 2018, Access Now reported that the Rajasthan state government gave police permission to conduct statewide internet shutdowns to avoid cheating during exams for constables, which left the entire region without internet for two days.
These shutdowns have occurred for a variety of examinations over the years, garnering frustration from residents whose lives have been put on pause during them.
In 2021, CNN, said that a shutdown was enforced during the Rajasthan Eligibility Examination for Teachers (REET), leaving 25 million people without internet for a full day. MediaNama reported on this as well, and cited the Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC), an Indian digital rights organization, who said this act was illegal and that these shutdowns harm the economy, education, healthcare and additional welfare schemes.
In 2024, MediaNama said that the exam shutdowns had become normalized in the state in their report on another shutdown that had been implemented to prevent paper leaks, despite the impact they have on the daily lives of residents.
Manipur Shutdowns: Conflict and Control
Manipur is a state in the northeastern part of India that is projected to be home to about 3.3 million people. The region has undergone intense ethnic conflicts since 2023, and accounts for 75 of India’s shutdowns since 2016, ranking third amongst the areas with highest frequency rates.
In 2023, the region saw its largest spike in internet shutdowns, with Access Now having recorded 48 events that year. Before this, Manipur had only experienced one to two shutdowns a year, if any, since Access Now began recording it.
This rise coincided with the timing of the ethnic clashes between the Meitei and Kuki communities, which spiraled into violent clashes on May 3, 2023. This date also marked the start of a total internet shutdown that lasted over 200 days, with some sources reporting that it continued until December 2023.
The SFLC said that this shutdown, which remains one of the longest recorded in the country, impacted peoples’ ability to pay rent, register for exams, access educational resources and complete their daily work.
The shutdown also kept the reality of the violence in Manipur hidden from the public, with much of India and the world unaware of the extent of the violence for weeks. According to TIME, many heard of it for the first time nearly 80 days after the clashes began when a video of two unclothed Kuki women being paraded around the streets by armed Meitei men was released.
The recording, which was discovered to have been taken on May 4, sparked global outrage. In light of the footage and ongoing shutdown, Reuters published an article detailing the impact the internet shutdown had on women’s ability to report human rights abuses like those endured by the women in the footage, leaving them without sufficient support, interference or justice.
In response to the backlash, the BJP claimed that the shutdown was done to avoid rumors and disinformation, as well as to quash the growth of fighting.
Today, clashes between these two groups continue despite government claims that shutdowns would lessen violence.
Broader Implications of Digital India and Internet Shutdowns
While the Digital India initiative promised connectivity across the nation, the internet shutdowns experienced by these three regions reflect a different reality for select parts of the country.
Despite experiencing these shutdowns under different social and political circumstances, J&K, Rajasthan and Manipur have dealt with the same negative effects fueled by the removal of internet and digital communications.
Each region has dealt with different levels of disruptions to their economies, businesses, daily life and communications, as well as access to education and healthcare, all the while suffering digital and human rights abuses that often occur in the dark.
As Digital India progresses and the internet continues to become a more integral part of society, these shutdowns will increasingly function as weapons with wide-ranging consequences for the people affected.
Methodology

The majority of the quantitative data used in this report comes from the Access Now STOP dataset between the years of 2016-2025. This data was analyzed in a jupyter notebook using a combination of python and pandas. When working with the STOP data in jupyter, the shutdowns with unknown end dates were marked as a day long, and those that are still ongoing were given an end date of ‘today’. This was done in an attempt to standardize the number of days recorded, and to not overestimate or downplay the number of shutdowns, which Access Now has said is likely lower than the true number of instances.

The “Individuals using the Internet (% by population) - India” dataset from the World Bank was also used to show the growth of internet usage throughout the country following Digital India’s launch in 2015. This was done to show how increasingly impactful these internet shutdowns are as more of the nation relies on it to operate in their daily lives and connect with the rest of their country.

Articles from various sources were also included in this report to provide context for the specific shutdowns discussed, as well as offer additional background on India and its shutdowns. All articles have been hyperlinked throughout the text.
